faq.a: They permanently disable the enzyme, so the body must synthesize new enzyme, leading to prolonged effects.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV patient on lopinavir/ritonavir develops elevated liver enzymes after starting rifampicin — What is the likely mechanism? — Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, reducing lopinavir levels and causing hepatotoxicity.
A 50‑year‑old man on warfarin presents with bruising after starting ciprofloxacin — What should you do? — Check INR, consider dose adjustment or switch antibiotics.
A child with malaria is given chloroquine; he develops seizures — What enzyme is likely inhibited? — Chloroquine inhibits Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase in neurons, causing neurotoxicity.
A patient on statins develops myalgia and elevated CK; you suspect drug interaction — Which enzyme pathway is involved? — CYP3A4 inhibition by another drug (e.g., clarithromycin).
A pregnant woman on aspirin develops epistaxis; you suspect platelet dysfunction — Which enzyme is inhibited? — Cyclooxygenase‑1, reducing thromboxane A₂.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B is started on tenofovir; later he develops renal dysfunction — Which enzyme system is implicated? — Tenofovir inhibits mitochondrial DNA polymerase, causing tubular toxicity.
ai.title: Enzyme Inhibition in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Enzyme inhibition is the cornerstone of many drugs and toxins. Clinicians must recognise how inhibitors alter metabolism, predict drug interactions, and identify toxicities, especially where laboratory support is limited.

sections.p: Enzyme inhibition reduces or stops the catalytic activity of an enzyme. In medicine it explains how many drugs work, how toxins cause disease, and why drug interactions occur.

b: IC50 is the concentration for 50% inhibition
sections.p: In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, preventing substrate binding. Non‑competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere, changing enzyme shape. Irreversible inhibitors form covalent bonds, permanently disabling the enzyme.

t.b: A 50% reduction at low µM suggests a potent inhibitor

sections.p: The body regulates enzyme activity via feedback, transcriptional control, and post‑translational modifications. Drugs exploit these pathways to achieve therapeutic effects.

t.b: High‑activity allele may need higher dose; low‑activity allele risks toxicity

sections.p: Inhibition can be therapeutic or harmful. Over‑inhibition of essential enzymes causes metabolic blocks; under‑inhibition leads to resistance. Toxins often irreversibly inhibit key enzymes.
Recognise drug classes that inhibit enzymes (e.g., protease inhibitors, statins, antiretrovirals) and their interactions. In low‑resource settings, monitor for signs of toxicity when labs are scarce.

t.a: Co‑administration of rifampicin and protease inhibitors

b: Ask about current meds before prescribing
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to predict interactions, interpret lab abnormalities, and choose appropriate monitoring. Focus on mechanism, clinical presentation, and management.

t.a: Patient on warfarin develops rash after starting ciprofloxacin
t.b: Check INR and consider dose adjustment

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause: stop the offending agent, provide supportive care, and monitor relevant parameters. Use antidotes when available (e.g., pralidoxime for organophosphates).

t.b: Supports diagnosis and guides antidote use

sections.p: Enzyme induction (increased activity) and enzyme activation (enzymes becoming active) are distinct from inhibition.
Some inhibitors cause transient lab changes that may be misinterpreted as disease. For example, statin‑induced myopathy can mimic polymyositis.

t.b: Rule out inflammatory myopathy with ANA

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained multi‑organ failure after starting a new medication
